title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease.
authors: Liu Xiaoyan; Du Xuguang; Qi Shihong; Yuan Lin; Liu Liyu et al.
abstract: Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

title: Bacteria inside kidney tumors associate with myeloid inflammation and disease progression: A TRACERx Renal study.
authors: Martin Alice C; Cattin Anne-Laure; Lockwood Parise K; Zepeda-Rivera Martha A; Becker Clara et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Intratumoral bacteria are increasingly recognized as active contributors to neutrophil-driven inflammation and disease progression in solid tumors. Yet, in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), where myeloid inflammation is a key feature of aggressive disease, live bacterial presence, their intratumoral distribution, and interaction with the tumor microenvironment remain unexplored.
METHODS: We genetically characterized the microbiome of primary ccRCC tumors across two independent cohorts (TRACERx: 616 samples, 143 patients; The Cancer Genome Atlas [TCGA]: 511 samples and patients), confirming live bacterial presence through culture. Multi-regional sampling enabled within-tumor analysis of bacterial distribution. Associations with the tumor microenvironment were explored at scale using bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) across both cohorts and corroborated in depth through spatial transcriptomics and in vitro infection assays.
FINDINGS: Across both cohorts, the commensal Cutibacterium emerged as the dominant genus, accumulating in discrete niches enriched toward the tumor center and associating with more advanced (TRACERx p = 0.024; TCGA p = 0.0011) tumors and shorter progression-free survival (TRACERx p = 0.0022; TCGA p = 4.4 × 10-4). Both across and within tumors, Cutibacterium accumulation associated with neutrophil recruitment and myeloid inflammation. In vitro, Cutibacterium induced sustained expression of neutrophil-attracting chemokines in macrophages, recapitulating patient tumor findings.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings establish intratumoral bacteria as novel prognostic components of the ccRCC tumor microenvironment and suggest an active role in shaping local myeloid inflammation, laying the groundwork for investigating their potential as therapeutic targets.
FUNDING: This work was supported by the Francis Crick Institute (Cancer Research UK, MRC, Wellcome Trust). TRACERx Renal is funded by Cancer Research UK (C50947/A18176).

title: Metagenomic Insights into Microplastic Micro-interfaces: Transforming Pollutants and Spreading Resistance.
authors: Tian Hongyu; Liu Jianwei; Zhang Yuxiu
abstract: Microplastic micro-interfaces (MPMI) in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) serve as critical hubs for microbial colonization, pollutant transformation, and antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) dissemination. In this study, a large-scale genome-resolved metagenomic approach was employed to reconstruct 463 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from biofilms established on polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyethylene (PE), and polypropylene (PP) within a municipal WWTP. Taxonomic profiling revealed that MPMI selectively enriched strict anaerobes and uncultured taxa, driving a profound ecological shift from the surrounding water and indicating the formation of localized hypoxic micro-niches. Functionally, the MPMI microbiome constructed a highly integrated metabolic network. Key dominant lineages were found to synergistically couple aromatic hydrocarbon degradation (via the shikimate pathway and β-oxidation) with complex carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling, while deploying energy-efficient nucleotide salvage strategies to ensure biofilm stabilization under nutrient stress. Crucially, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) emerged as a fundamental mechanism for functional diversification, facilitating the active cross-genomic exchange of key adaptive traits associated with pollutant metabolism and biofilm regulation. Furthermore, MPMI harbored a highly diverse resistome comprising 36 ARG categories and 289 subtypes, highlighted by the critical genomic co-localization of mobile elements and clinical resistance markers (e.g., mcr-5.1, mupA) in core colonizers. Ultimately, these genomic insights elucidate the MPMI as a profound ecological hotspot driving the concurrent adaptation of metabolic networks and the resistome, thereby exacerbating the risks of ARG dissemination in aquatic environments.

title: Microbiome interactions in renal cell carcinoma: evidence, challenges and opportunities.
authors: Lindgaard Cecilie; Hvidt Astrid Korning; Keller Anna Krarup; Thingholm Louise; Kristensen Sara Schou et al.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a heterogeneous malignancy with limited predictive biomarkers to guide treatment. Emerging evidence suggests that the microbiome might influence systemic immunity, therapeutic response and clinical outcomes. In metastatic RCC, the gut microbiome has been linked to the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, whereas the existence of a tumour microbiome remains a topic of debate. Circulating microbial DNA in blood has been proposed as a minimally invasive window into systemic immune status, offering a potential tool for monitoring treatment response, but its role in RCC is largely unexplored. Evidence from mechanistic studies, primarily from other solid cancer types, suggests that microbiome-immune crosstalk, microbial metabolites and functionally redundant pathways across taxa could modulate tumour biology. However, progress in RCC microbiome research remains limited by small cohorts, methodological variability and challenges in working with samples with a low microbial biomass, which are highly prone to contamination. Emerging spatial and multi-omics technologies now enable high-resolution mapping of these complex interactions, offering the potential to transform our understanding of the cancer microbiome. A structured roadmap is required to overcome technical and analytical challenges in RCC microbiome studies, enabling the identification of clinically relevant microbial signatures and their role in shaping tumour immunity.

title: Engineering adaptive polysaccharide biomaterials: integrated biotechnology framework for regenerative medicine.
authors: Ali Sameh S; Khan Kashif; Hassan Hend Elkahlawy; Ali Asmaa; El Aziz Fatma Abd et al.
abstract: Natural polysaccharides are versatile building blocks for regenerative biomaterials because of their structural diversity, generally favorable biocompatibility and biodegradability, chemical tunability, and capacity for biologically relevant interactions. Advances in biotechnology and materials engineering have expanded their role from primarily structural matrices to multifunctional platforms that can influence cellular, immune, and biochemical processes during tissue repair. This review presents an integrated biological engineering framework linking polysaccharide source and molecular architecture with extraction and purification, chemical functionalization, crosslinking, advanced fabrication, biological recognition, and translational performance. Particular emphasis is placed on structure-function relationships, stereospecific glycan-receptor interactions, immune-instructive biomaterials, protein-mediated cell-material interactions, microbiome-responsive systems, and emerging artificial intelligence-assisted approaches for biomaterial design. The importance of material purity is also critically considered, particularly the potential for residual endotoxin contamination to confound interpretation of immunomodulatory responses and compromise reproducibility. Representative applications in skin, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, neural, and other regenerative systems illustrate how material composition, scaffold architecture, biofunctionalization, and manufacturing strategy collectively influence biological performance. Finally, challenges associated with scalable manufacturing, batch-to-batch reproducibility, sterilization, storage stability, quality control, regulatory translation, and clinical implementation are examined. By integrating molecular design, biological mechanisms, fabrication, and translational requirements, this review provides engineering principles for the development of adaptive polysaccharide biomaterials and identifies priorities for advancing reproducible and clinically translatable regenerative technologies.

title: Gut virome remodeling after fecal microbiota transplantation is associated with virus-bacteria co-variation and metabolic response in obesity and type 2 diabetes.
authors: Jiang Hui; Peng Ye; Lam Brian; Yang Keli; Lin Yu et al.
abstract: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) modifies gut bacterial composition and improves metabolic outcomes in subjects with obesity and type 2 diabetes (ObT2), but bacterial changes alone do not fully explain the heterogeneity in clinical response. We performed virus-like particle (VLP)-enriched metagenomic sequencing coupled with bulk-DNA metagenomic sequencing on longitudinal fecal samples from a randomized controlled FMT trial in ObT2. Using random forest classification, post-FMT virome changes showed accuracy comparable to bacteriome changes (84.8% vs 81.4%) in distinguishing LDL responders from non-responders. Donor-derived viral contig engraftment was detected in 64.7% (11/17) of recipients receiving FMT alone and 58.8% (10/17) receiving FMT with lifestyle intervention (LSI), versus 5.6% (1/18) in the sham with LSI group. FMT was associated with increased virome diversity, compositional shifts toward the donor virome, and coordinated virus-bacteria associations, with most responsive viral contigs classified as Caudoviricetes. FMT-responsive viral contigs that were shared between the two FMT groups were predicted to infect Roseburia and Bifidobacterium, while contigs associated with clinical responses were predicted to infect Escherichia, Roseburia, Blautia, and Enterococcus. These findings suggest that the gut virome is a complementary ecological component associated with FMT responses and metabolic outcomes in ObT2.

title: Amino acid availability influences Staphylococcus aureus interaction with the nasal microbiota in a strain- and community-specific manner.
authors: Camus Laura; Franz Jessica; Gerlach David; Lange Anna; Power Jeffrey John et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Only some individuals carry Staphylococcus aureus in the nose, predisposing them to endogenous infections. While microbial cooperation and competition are known to shape environmental and intestinal microbial communities, their impact on pathogen colonization within the nasal microbiome is largely unknown.
RESULTS: Using a newly curated nasal strain collection and systematic pairwise interaction analysis, we investigated competitive and collaborative traits between diverse S. aureus strains and nasal communities. Our experiments revealed that nasal species strongly modulate S. aureus growth in a strain- and community-specific manner both in vitro and in gnotobiotic mice. Nutrient-dependent interactions emerged as key drivers. In one example, we found that tyrosine provided by synthetic communities supported proliferation of an auxotrophic S. aureus strain. Screening of a large collection of S. aureus strains identified tyrosine dependency in 8% of strains, with colonization impaired in the absence of supportive communities, indicating broader relevance of this interaction.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal distinct metabolic adaptations that enable S. aureus to exploit specific features of resident nasal communities, highlighting complex interspecies networks that influence colonization in the human nose. These insights may inform microbiome-editing strategies to displace S. aureus from the nasal niche. Video Abstract.

title: From ecosystem engineering to living computers: integrating dual-paradigm bacterial therapeutics for solid tumor microenvironment reprogramming.
authors: Elmetwalli Alaa; Algehainy Naseh A; Altemani Faisal H; Alanazi Mohammad A; Altemani Abdullah H
abstract: Recent advances in tumor microbiome biology and synthetic biology have made bacteria attractive therapeutic agents capable of reprogramming tumor-associated microbial ecosystems and serving as programmable living systems in solid tumors. In this review, we construct a dual-paradigm framework combining engineered bacterial therapeutics and ecosystem editing. In the first paradigm, phage-mediated targeting, competitive displacement, and metabolic reprogramming are used to alter tumor-associated microbial communities. In the second paradigm, engineered bacteria are equipped with environmental sensors, genetic logic circuits, and therapeutic payloads. We discuss the mechanistic interplay of these strategies in terms of ecological niche formation, bacterial colonization, immune and metabolic remodeling, and microbiome-host feedback. Clinical experience still varies across platforms due to differences in bacterial strain, attenuation, route of administration, tumor biology, treatment context, and patient characteristics. Major translational challenges include biocontainment, genetic stability, manufacturing and potency control, predictive biomarker validation, and product-specific regulatory requirements. We propose an additional hypothesis-generating framework for patient stratification and adaptive treatment monitoring. These concepts together provide a structured framework for exploring bacterial therapeutics as components of precision oncology, while highlighting the need for prospective clinical validation.

title: A stratified human colon model reveals SCFA cross-feeding-driven host-microbe dynamics associated with epithelial and immune responses.
authors: Kim Taewon; Park Joon-Young; Kim Minae; Kim Na Young; Jang Seol-A et al.
abstract: Host-microbe interactions are essential for maintaining intestinal homeostasis, yet most in vitro models lack physiological oxygen gradients, mucosal architecture, and reproducibility. We developed the Mucosal Mimetic 3D-Host Aerobic Microbiota Anaerobic Co-culture (Mm 3D-HaeMan) system, a colon-mimetic, oxygen-stratified platform enabling stable co-culture of colonic epithelial cells, human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (hPBMCs), and obligate anaerobes. Oxygen profiling confirmed a stable gradient consistent with human colonic stratification. Using a canonical short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) cross-feeding pair (Anaerostipes caccae and Bifidobacterium bifidum, AcBb consortium), we performed integrated, multilayered analyzes of the host-microbe interface. Co-culture with the SCFA-producing AcBb consortium was associated with enhanced epithelial-mitochondrial respiration, maintenance of transepithelial resistance, tight junction protein expression without barrier disruption, and rebalanced cytokine profiles. Host transcriptomics identified 41 differentially expressed genes (15 upregulated, 26 downregulated) associated with homeostatic-relevant epithelial responses. Simultaneously, bacterial metatranscriptomics revealed 29 differentially expressed gene families; notably, glaK was enriched in bacteria-only cultures; SORD, nuoG, and nuoE were specifically induced during co-culture, indicating host-associated bacterial transcriptional changes. The compartmentalized design permits independent sampling for layer-resolved multi-omics and functional readouts. These findings establish Mm 3D-HaeMan as a physiologically grounded platform for dissecting bidirectional host-microbe responses and immune-associated interactions. This model offers broad applicability for mechanistic research and translational screening of probiotics and microbiome-based therapeutics.
